utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning. May we begin in the usual manner by having the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the Prosecution I'm Thomas Hannis joined by Matthew Olmsted and our case manager Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Stanisic Defence Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There was one procedural matter I wanted to raise first thing this morning. It concerns Witness ST-110 Mr. Trbojevic. He's here pursuant to a subpoena issued by the Trial Chamber, but in light of the pace at which we have been proceeding we had anticipated he would start to testify today or tomorrow, but now it looks like he wouldn't begin before next week. He is a practising lawyer, he has some cases which he is counsel for and scheduled to appear in state court in Bosnia next week. We would propose if the Court is willing to allow him to return home today or tomorrow as scheduled by victim witness and return at a later date. We are suggesting perhaps the week of November 23rd. But because he's here under subpoena issued by you, we felt it necessary to bring him here to court. If you're willing to go along with our suggestion then we would ask to have him brought in and be advised by the Court that he remains under the subpoena and that he will have to return the week of November 23rd. I think -- I've had some discussion with Mr. Zecevic, and I believe the Defence does not oppose this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have no objection. We understand the situation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, for how long time was Mr. ST-110 supposed to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure what we put in our notification last week, but he is a 92 ter. I'd estimated perhaps three hours with direct, and the Defence, I think Mr. Zecevic had said five -- oh, I see he's giving me the signal of eight hours now on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One hour. So this seems to me that ST-110 would have to stay here for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the reason we can't hear him, I understand, is that we have another subpoenaed witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. ST-111. Now, for how long was he scheduled to testify. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not -- my case manager's checking for me. Three hours, and I believe the original estimate I'd seen from the Defence I think was six hours for Mr. Zecevic and one hour for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So again we have subpoenaed a witness who is required to testify over several days. Now, if I am not mistaken, you asked the Court to issue subpoena orders on two consecutive days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe there were -- they were scheduled two days apart. One was scheduled to appear on Tuesday and one on Thursday. I'm not sure, but that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And part of that is done, Your Honour in case the first witness is not served and doesn't respond to the subpoena. We didn't want to have too big a gap in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Do you suggest you bring him into the courtroom, or what was your plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe victim witness had him brought over today. I'm not sure which waiting-room he's in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, can I just inquire whether you wanted to bring him to the courtroom and have the Court admonish him that now he goes home but he has to promise us that he will return upon a new call?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did that just based on practice in my domestic jurisdiction. I didn't feel I had the authority to tell him that the Court says you can go home but you have to come back on this date. Our practice where I came from was to have the witness brought in and be admonished by the Court that you are still under the subpoena, you are going to be allowed to go home now but you have to return on such and such a date. If you don't, the penalties that you were warned about remain in effect and could be imposed against you in the event that you do not return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That, too, is my practice, my experience, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. So let's bring him in. Mr. Hannis, if we can't find him, I suggest we just start with the other witness and then take Mr. ST-110 at the beginning of the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the victim witness was advised yesterday, the witness was advised yesterday to be here this morning. I assumed that the usual transport was arranged, and I assume he's in one of the victim waiting rooms, but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, he doesn't have to make the declaration. Good morning, sir. Please have a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You would have been brought here today, or you -- the reason why you're here today is because the Tribunal would have issued a subpoena requiring your attendance. For reasons that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For reasons that you may or may not be aware of -- as you would be, I'm sure, be familiar with the process of trials whereby it isn't always possible to predict the progress of a particular trial and therefore from time to time delays, unfortunately, occur to the inconvenience of, in this case, witnesses and those who are -- would prefer to be elsewhere. The -- we're advised by the Prosecution, at whose instance you were subpoenaed, that the schedule is such that they are unable to lead your evidence today. You, nevertheless, are still under the requirement to attend before the Tribunal according to the subpoena, and it is proposed -- well, we intend to release you today, and it is proposed that you return here on the 23rd of November when the Prosecution would be ready for you. Do you understand what I've said so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we regret the inconvenience caused and the disruption to your personal schedule, but you're now free to return and continue -- to return to your home and continue your ordinary domestic and personal dealings, but you are directed to return to this Chamber on the 23rd of November. Arrangements -- the usual arrangements will be made to facilitate your attendance on that date. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one correction. I made a misstatement. We announced five hours for cross of Mr. Trbojevic. I said eight, and I saw that His Honour Judge Delvoie was looking at me with -- with a look of unbelief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate that. Mr. Olmsted will be calling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution is ready to call the next witness. The next witness has been granted protective measures, both a pseudonym as well as image distortion. Perhaps while --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps while we're waiting for the witness to come in I could give a brief summary of his prior testimony just to put his testimony here today into context. In his Rule 92 ter statement, ST-79 describes events surrounding the armed attack on Visegrad by the JNA Uzice Corps in April 1992. He tells how Muslim houses were targeted for looting and destruction by Serb paramilitary groups, and that the JNA and local Serbs established check-points around the municipality at which Muslims were stopped to determine whether they were on lists. The witness further describes how Serb forces took Muslims from their homes and places of employment and describes his own arrest on 7 June 1992 by Milan Lukic who was wearing a police uniform that day, and three other armed Serbs. They took the witness and six other Muslim men to the Drina River near Visegrad, made them line up along the bank and opened fire on them, killing five of the Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it appears that the witness has protective measures. I rely on the list the Prosecution sent to us with the daily witnesses and so on, and there it is mentioned that there are no protective measures. So I would be glad if that list would be -- could be accurate in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll make sure that it is accurate in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And thank you for coming to the Tribunal. You are called here as a witness in the case against Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin, and the first thing we would like you to do is to read the solemn declaration to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you may sit down. Sir, as I told you, you have been called by the Prosecution to testify in this case, and the first thing that is going to happen is that the Prosecution will put some questions to you, and you will then be asked questions by the Defence, but first of all, let us start by going into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. As I just said, you have been accorded protective measures, a pseudonym and face distortion, which means that people from outside this courtroom cannot see your face and cannot hear your name because the name that we will use for you will be ST-79. So from this moment on, we will address you, Mr. Witness, ST-79. As I said, you have been called to testify under an expediated procedure meaning that the Prosecution will put a few questions to you lasting no more than 30 minutes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Defence for Mr. Stanisic will then put questions to you lasting altogether approximately -- how long time was it, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was advised that Mr. O'Sullivan will conduct the cross-examination, that it would last around half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have question for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So this is the schedule for today. The Prosecution will take you through your testimony in about half an hour, and we will then give the floor to Mr. O'Sullivan who is representing Mico Stanisic, and he, too, will use about 30 minutes, and that will be the end of your testimony. So thank you very much, Mr. Witness. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And good morning, ST-79.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: ST-79, did you provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I'm sorry, I forgot to have the witness sign his name sheet, so could you please arrange that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May the usher provide him the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. ST-79, can you confirm that this is the name that appears on the sheet before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would you then please just sign it and give it back to the usher. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. ST-79, did you provide your testimony in the Lukic case on 10 and 11 July, 2008?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And since arriving here in The Hague to testify here, have you had the opportunity to listen to that testimony from the Lukic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were the tapes that you listened to an accurate reflection of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions here today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this witness's Rule 92 ter statement, which is 65 ter exhibit numbers 10046.1 and 10046.2 and associated exhibits 65 ter numbers 3449, 3450 and 3451 be admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pseudonym sheet of the witness will become Exhibit P174 under seal, and the documents which form the part of the 92 ter package will become Exhibit P175.1 through P175.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. ST-79, I would like to ask you some questions that clarify and expand upon the issues that you addressed during your prior testimony, and first of all, during your prior testimony you describe how upon returning to Visegrad at the end of April 1992, after the Uzice Corps had taken control of the town, you encountered a number of check-points around Visegrad. You also state that the check-points were manned by a mix of JNA soldiers and local Serbs and that some of these local Serbs were wearing police uniforms. Could you describe for us the police uniforms that you saw these local Serbs wearing at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, these were standard issue police uniforms. I can't at this moment tell you exactly -- see any colours that are similar, but they were -- the shirt was light blue and the pants were darker but also blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And would they wear any insignias or patches on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. On the sleeve there had to be insignia, the police and what town it belonged to or what municipality. The same way that insignia is worn nowadays on uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned during your prior testimony that the persons manning these check-points had lists of names that they checked against the people they stopped. From what you could observe, what were the ethnicities of the persons on these lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: They were Muslim by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Serbs arrested or harassed at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In addition to these check-points, what other movement restrictions were imposed upon the Bosniaks in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was hard to move around because of the White Eagles operation at the time. It was difficult to move around and to even stay there, because they took people of Muslim nationality out of companies, or they took them away from their homes, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were some Muslims required to report at certain locations on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances. I know of a case. This was very soon after my return from Gorazde. Some neighbours of mine who had probably been arrested earlier when the Uzice Corps entered the town, I don't know exactly who actually arrested people at the time, but in any case, this was after my return from Gorazde. There was this circle of people that I played cards with, and they said that they had to report to the SUP at the time every hour or every other hour, but who this was who issued that order and to whom they had to report, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When these neighbours of yours would return from the police station, would there be any change in their physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't notice that they had been beaten or anything of that sort, but they just had to report there to make sure that they were still in that town lest they move out, maybe join a paramilitary formation or just escape to a wood. But in any case, I know they hadn't been beaten then, but I know that one or two of them, as far as I know, had been liquidated, had been killed. They had gone to SUP to report, and they never returned, and to this day they are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also state during your prior testimony, and I think you've just mentioned a little while ago that Muslims were taken from their places of work during this April to May 1992 time period, and I think you also mentioned that it was the White Eagles who were doing this. Were the police aware that the White Eagles were going around and arresting people at their places of employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, Visegrad is a small town, so they would have had to be aware of it. They knew what was going on in the town. And if Your Honours allow me, I could give a few examples of how the police operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the Trial Chamber will have some questions regarding that, or maybe it will come out as I ask further questions. The families of the Muslims who were taken away by the White Eagles, did they complain to the police or someone else regarding these arrests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. The wives and the mothers went to the then SUP to complain that their men had been taken away, or their brothers or husbands, and to this they received the reply that the police did not have any control over those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides these arrests of Muslims from their places of employment, what other activities were the White Eagles engaging in throughout Visegrad during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, to me, I can't find the right word. There was general chaos. They would steal cars from people. They would take people away. They would sometimes play the screams of people who had been tortured, riding around town in these cars. So they would tour the town and play these horrible screams through the loudspeakers. I think probably to terrorise people. I don't know. To instill fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: From what you could see, what were the police doing to prevent the White Eagles from engaging in these kind of activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, they did not interfere in any way. They never tried to punish anyone or to prevent any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What level of trust did you have and your family have and other Bosniaks in the community in which you live have in the police in ensuring the security of your families and homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was no trust whatsoever either in the police or the army. To me it all seemed that these White Eagles who were doing this throughout the town, and even while the Uzice Corps was there, it appeared to me that they were under their protection, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to show you a couple of photographs. The first one is 65 ter Exhibit number 10140. Now, sir, do you recognise either man in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. The man on the right, as I see it, is Milan Lukic. He's in a camouflage uniform. And we can also see this Passat vehicle. That's the vehicle that I was driven away in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is this how Milan Lukic looked back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: No. He did have a uniform but not this one. This is a green camouflage uniform, whereas he had a blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With -- take a look at the other man in the photograph, the man on the left. And perhaps we can zoom in a little bit further on him. I'm just curious. You can see on his left arm he has a patch or an insignia. Have you ever seen that insignia before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. I think that insignia was on the uniform that Lukic wore at the time. Now, I can't see here whether it says "Police" on the patch or something else, but this is what it looked like approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, back during this time period, other than police would the insignia also say something to the effect of "Milicija"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. When Lukic came to take me out of my house, I think he had a patch on his left shoulder. I can't really recall precisely, but I think it says "Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you -- you say you recognise the vehicle as the vehicle that you were taken away from your home on 7 June 1992. Who was the original owner of that vehicle that you see in this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: The owner of this vehicle was Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you know, what happened to this woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Lukic killed her in her own apartment and stole her car.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise the place where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I couldn't really -- I'm not certain. I think it's a part of the town, but I'm not sure which part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph is not on our 65 ter exhibit list yet. I'm not sure if the Defence opposes its admission at this stage. Does the Defence oppose us seeking to admit this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we admit it then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, just to be clear, we're talking here -- the witness is talking about police and about White Eagles, and then he's telling us about Lukic in a blue police uniform. Does he mean White Eagle or police?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I understand your question, you're wondering whether Milan Lukic was with the White Eagles or the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You can put the question to the witness if you like. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: ST-79, do you know whether Milan Lukic was with the White Eagles or with the police? Were you aware of his employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, when he came to take me away, he had a blue camouflage uniform on, and on the patch it said on his sleeve, it said "Police." Now, as far as I knew, he was in the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another photograph. It's Rule 65 ter Exhibit number 10139.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at the photograph on the bottom, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. The upper row on the left is Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if you can take a look at the man squatting down in the front row to the right with the sunglasses. He also has a patch or an insignia on his left arm. Perhaps we can zoom in on that a little bit. I'm just wondering if you'd ever see that kind of patch or insignia around Visegrad during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, I think that's the patch that we discussed a little earlier. They were both not very visible, so I can't really state with certainty, and I can't claim that they are the same, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but would you say that that -- I know you can't see it perfectly clear, but does that at least resemble the patch of a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again this document isn't on our 65 ter exhibit list, but because it's a photograph perhaps the Defence doesn't oppose us admitting it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, during your prior testimony you state that you were -- while you were on your way to the Vilina Vlas Hotel in a car driven by Milan Lukic, you were stopped at a check-point. Could you tell us who was manning that check-point at which you were stopped in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. This was a check-point in Sase, close to Vilina Vlas. There was an intersection there, a fork in the road, and the -- he stopped the car there. There was a check-point there. A police man was standing there, and Lukic said to him and I quote, "I've caught myself some Balijas."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How did the police officer manning the check-point react to this statement by Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as I could hear, there was no mention of why he had done that, but as far as I could observe, this policeman was also proud of this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you a map and have you mark certain locations on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we look at 65 ter Exhibit 10141.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I think Mr. Usher is going to show you how to use the digital pen. First -- first, can you identify where this police check-point we were just describing at Sase was on your way to the Vilina Vlas Hotel. If you can mark it with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You marked it. Could you put a big number 1 next to it just so we can reference it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. And next could you mark with a number 2 the rough location of the Vilina Vlas Hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. Now, if you could mark with a number 3 the place along the River Drina that you and the other Bosniak men were taken by Milan Lukic and his men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Approximately how far is this location from that check-point in Sase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, I think I stated that in my statement. About 200 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And on this day where this crime incident which you describe in your statement occurred, in your line along the River Drina, obviously there might have been noises coming from the group that you were with, but beyond that did you hear any other sounds in the area surrounding you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes, because there were the -- the weapons were being fired intermittently in bursts, and then individual shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that was within the group that you were with along the River Drina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question to you is: Beyond the group that you were with, maybe in the distance or near the houses nearby or anywhere around you, did you hear any other sounds while you were standing there on the bank of the River Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, yes. You could hear gunfire, and you could see -- you could hear cars passing and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I think we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, but it looks like there was a technical problem and he has to go back and mark the two prior locations on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, could you, once again, mark with a number 1 the location of the Sase check-point and with a number 2 the location of the Vilina Vlas Hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, in your statement you mentioned that after you escaped the execution at the Drina, you crossed the river and then later you observed the corpses from a hill. Can you mark with a number 4 where that location on the hill was that you observed the corpses from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you observed these corpses from the hill, was that on the same day of the crime incident or was it subsequent to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, this was on the next day, the day after. I spent that night in a house in that village, and then I took my neighbours and these people to -- to the place where I was supposed to be shot, and then I saw these bodies, these corpses that were in the water, and they were there for the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from this hill across the River Drina that you observed these corpses from, how clearly could you see the corpses from that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, you see, you couldn't tell who they were. You couldn't recognise their faces, but it was clearly visible that these were bodies of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can take a look at the map. Along the right side -- sorry, the left side of the River Drina, just below the hill that you observed the corpses from there is a road that appears. Could you see the corpses from that road as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. This was the road leading to Barimo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did hear the next place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you tell us -- the interpreter didn't hear your full statement. Could you tell us where that road led to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: This road led to Barimo, Milosevici, Brstanica, and so on, these various hamlets that were down the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the bodies were -- remained along the River Drina bank for a couple of days. Can you tell us how you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, I crossed the river -- well, actually, I went from this hill every single day to observe this, because everyone was interested to see where it was that I had been taken and how many people had been shot, killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know what happened eventually to those corpses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, probably when the river withdrew -- the level of the river could change because they had control over this because there was a dam in Bajina Basta, so once there were a lot of bodies there they would close the lake, the accumulation lake, and then the water would come and take these bodies down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours may this map be admitted into evidence as marked by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally, my final topic with you, ST-79. Could you tell us who Sredoje Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic was a police officer in Visegrad. That's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We definitely need Courtroom I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about, first of all, the uniforms that the White Eagles wore. I believe you have described them as camouflage uniforms on which there were double-headed Eagles on the front pocket. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you saw Milan Lukic for the first time in June 1992, he was wearing a uniform that had the double-headed eagle on the uniform, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also noticed on that uniform that there was a police insignia, but you don't know which police insignia; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. It was written "Policija," but I don't know what sort of marking was there. Was it the one of the former Yugoslavia or these other ones, I don't know. All I know is that the marking was "Policija," "Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew that Mr. Lukic was originally from Visegrad, and you believed that he worked in the police in Obrenovac, Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the police in Serbia wear blue uniforms, don't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you -- you travelled in Serbia, didn't you, prior to the war? The police wore blue uniforms, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't travel in Serbia, and I don't know. They probably did wear them. I didn't have the opportunity to see how a policeman in Serbia was dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Didn't you know that the police in all of the former Yugoslavia wore blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. They wore blue uniforms. I don't know whether it was at the federal level. I guess if it was one state, then it probably had a uniform -- regulation uniform for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that the White Eagles were made up of Serbs from Serbia and local Serbs from Visegrad? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I think that's what I said in the statement, that there were both.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's correct, is it -- isn't it? I'm asking you to confirm your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct for the locals. I don't know for the other ones that I didn't know, but, yeah, it's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the White Eagles were made up mostly of younger men, and the local -- the locals were mostly older men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: That's not what I said in the statement. It says that the White Eagles comprised mainly younger men.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I may have misspoken. That's what I intended to say. The White Eagles were mostly younger men, and the locals were mostly older men. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: No. White Eagles would indicate younger men. The local men who were in the White Eagles were also younger men. For example, one of them who might recognise in front of the new hotel in Visegrad in the centre of town, I think that I refer to him as Oliver Krsmanovic. He was the only one whom I recognised there. At the time he was perhaps some 25 to 30 years old. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I think you've described the White Eagles as a very dangerous group that was out of control. Would that be a fair description of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And they were rather undisciplined; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it also be correct to say that they would abuse alcohol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So they were basically doing what they wanted, and they were not under anyone's control. Would that be a fair way to put it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time - I'm thinking about April, May, June 1992 - that there was a shortage of uniforms to go around for the people who were engaged in the conflict? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I don't know if there were enough uniforms. Most of the people were uniformed. I don't know whether there were enough uniforms or not, but there should have been enough, because everybody was wearing a uniform, even from the reserve forces. Even I had one from the reserve forces from before the war. So it probably was the case that they did have enough uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But not everyone would necessarily be wearing his uniform. Isn't it a fact that your former JNA uniform was taken away from you and probably given to someone else to wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we see from your evidence that Milan Lukic wore at least two types of uniforms, according to your testimony, two different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And didn't you also notice during that period that there were people who would have partial uniforms because they didn't have full uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that anywhere, that they had partial uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you if you ever saw that. I'm not asking you whether you said it before, but didn't you see that in the early days during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Perhaps there were such cases. I really didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Earlier today you were asked about people who were taken away from work. You remember you had the question from the Prosecutor a few minutes ago about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that you don't know who the people were that were taking people away from work? You don't know who was doing that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I don't know them by name, but I know by the stories of the people from the companies who were eyewitnesses of such things and that these things were done by the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you of what you said when you were a witness in the Lukic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's the -- for the record that's Lukic transcript pages 380, 381, which I believe is P175.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll read to you, sir, what you said in the Lukic case. You were asked this question: "Who was taking them away from your work?" And your answer: "I don't know. Probably those White Eagles or the paramilitary units that were there, that were there in Visegrad at the time." Next question is this: "Would it be fair to say instead of saying 'probably,' that you just don't know?" And you answered: -- and you answered yes, you didn't know. Now it's the true, isn't it, that you didn't know. You adopted this Lukic statement when you began your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes, that was it, but I'm testifying here on the basis of my best recollection. You have these statements in front of you, and I am sitting here and telling you what I remember. I'm remembering things that happened 17 years ago, so perhaps there are some little things that are not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. And what you said in the Lukic trial in 2001 -- or, sorry, 2008, was your best recollection. You told the truth when you said you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I probably did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You went to the police station in Visegrad once in 1992, in the month of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I don't recall the month, but I did go to the police station because my brother was arrested and beaten up at the police station, and I went to see if they would release him and when. However, he told me to just get away from there and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know that he was arrested and beaten up by the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you went to the police station that day, you only saw military personnel at the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I didn't even enter the police station. I was in front of the police station and my brother was at the window, and he indicated to me from the window to get away, that it wasn't safe, and I think that I said that perhaps there was a soldier there or something like that, but I don't think that I saw any police.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. You only saw military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have very limited re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, during your cross-examination you were asked questions about this double-headed eagle. Had you ever seen this double-headed eagle symbol before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I can explain that to you. It's probably a symbol of Serbdom, the two-headed eagle. This is what I can conclude. I had the opportunity to see that. In World War II, similar insignia was worn, so it wasn't the first time that I was seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So was this a symbol only of the White Eagles or did it represent something beyond that, and would you see it in other places around other people's uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you whether it was just the White Eagles that used it as the insignia. The Chetniks also wore that in World War II on their caps. It's probably some sort of insignia of a particular unit or indicating heroes. I don't know. I mean, I wasn't really interested, whether that was some kind of important symbol or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, when you're talking about the men who had been arrested and taken away from their places of employment, during your examination you were talking about how family members would go to the police station and inquire with the police what happened to their family members who were taken away. Do you recall what the police -- whether the police told the family members who was taking these people away, who was making these arrests?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object to that question. How would he know? How would he recall what the police said? He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You had testified earlier that family members went to the police station to inquire on Muslims who had been taken away from their employment. Did you ever learn from what they had found out at the police station as to who -- whether the police identified who was taking away these people from their places of employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-79
utterances.text: I just said that based on what I knew, that mothers and wives were leaving -- going to the MUP and saying that the White Eagles had taken their men away, and the police, according to what I know, would say that they had no control over those people, and I think this is the same thing that I said in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for attending. You are now released. You may return to your home. We wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for the confidence you have shown in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this would be an appropriate time for the break. Ms. Korner will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, but could we just raise one little matter before we go to the break, and that relates to the mode of admission into evidence of the whole batch of documents, I think it was 108 documents, relating to the next witness. As I recall, the Chamber ruled that in order for the Prosecution to have these documents admitted into evidence without having to go through each and every one of them with the witness, our proposal was to suggest that the Prosecution could perhaps divide the documents into groups and then present the witness with one or maybe two documents from each group so as to have the witness's comments to these documents as his oral evidence, but then if the Chamber was assured that the rest of the documents belonging to that group would -- had the same character as the document that was put to the witness, then we could admit that whole group and then move on to the next group. Now, I see that the Prosecution has offered such a grouping, a regrouping, of the documents, but the regrouping that you have done is a grouping according to the source, and I'm not sure if that is really useful, and I would ask if the Prosecution could perhaps regroup and do the same thing as Mr. Zecevic did when he was grouping his documents yesterday, namely to group them either according to municipality or to crimes, because that would enable us to -- to assess the -- the coherence between the documents in each of the groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll certainly convey that to Mrs. Korner. I know that she had done some grouping of the documents, and I do recall at least some of them were grouped by source. For example, I think one category was government sessions, meetings of the government, and the witness Mr. Djeric was the prime minister. That seemed to be a logical way for us to do it, because that dealt with the authenticity and such matters relating to that group all come from the same source, and so that seemed to make sense. And those meetings of the government sessions discuss a whole panoply of topics that cover several municipalities and different kinds of events. So it's hard for me standing here right now, Your Honour, to think of how we could break those down according to separate crimes or parts of the indictment. But I'll convey what you've just said to her, and we'll take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please do, because you realise that the difficulty that the Chamber will have in the end when we assess the evidence, is it will be difficult for us to -- to ascertain what the evidentiary value of the documents that we admit into evidence without having seen them really is. This is why it would be helpful if you would introduce one group of documents, say, relating to crimes committed in a particular municipality, or that you could perhaps group the documents according to one of the crimes or the crimes that are listed in your indictment, because that would enable us then to immediately assess the evidence for the purpose of -- of the deliberations after the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Some groups of documents are being offered for purposes other than the crimes, to show the interrelationship between the parties, the hierarchies and structures, and other matters as well that are important, and certainly when we are filing our final brief we would be pointing you to specific documents and things where we want to make arguments based on those documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honours. I was notified that the document I used yesterday, which was exhibited as 1D52, MFI'd because pending translations, we just received the translation this morning, and it has been uploaded, and therefore I kindly move the Trial Chamber to admit it as -- as a proper exhibit. Thank you very much. The translation has been uploaded in the e-court, and the court officer has been notified of the number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's now admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I was watching the proceedings, so I heard the remarks of Judge Harhoff at the end of the first session. Your Honours, can I explain that this witness, Mr. Djeric, was a member of the government of the Republika Srpska, or the Serbian republic in Bosnia as it began, from March of 1992 as prime minister, until the end of November when he resigned. The documents which he can speak to of us own knowledge are not divisible into the sort of categories that one can do with a witness who is giving evidence about actual crimes that were committed as to a certain extent was Mr. Krulj yesterday and the day before. The government, either in the Assembly or in its own meetings did not tend to discuss the specifics of crimes that were committed. The reason for calling this witness is twofold. We say that the documents which relate to the running of the Republika Srpska in 1992 are relevant largely to the joint criminal enterprise which the Prosecution allege, much to Mr. Pantelic's fury, took place in the course of 1992. All of those documents add, in little bits and pieces when put together to what we say is evidence of that joint criminal enterprise and which the Defence say, to the contrary, does not say any such thing and that's the issue between the two parties on this. Additionally, this witness will give evidence directly in respect of his dealings with Mico Stanisic, who was the minister of the interior. Accordingly the most sensible division that we could come up with in respect of these documents to comply with the way that Your Honours wish the documents to be dealt with was to divide them into categories of the Assembly minutes, the Presidency minutes, and I will ask Mr. Djeric to explain so that Your Honours fully understand the difference between the functions of the government, the NSC, the National Security Council and Presidency minutes there is one minute we're putting in through the National Security Council on its own. Then there was the Council of Ministers and the government minutes. Then there are documents which don't specifically fall into any of these categories but which he himself directly issued or received, a few miscellaneous - if I can put it that way - documents about which he can speak but wasn't personally concerned, and finally intercepts of which there are in fact five altogether. Only four when he listened to them were legible in which he was able to make identification of voices. The fifth we're trying to get enhanced at the moment and, if necessary, play it to him in court tomorrow when it's been enhanced. And so that is the division that we have done with those documents and on which -- the basis on which I have worked. It is my proposal to deal with something like 20-odd -- I actually added them up -- in a little detail, and then in accordance with Your Honours' ruling to submit the rest of the documents within these categories to be marked for identification subject to cross-examination by Mr. Zecevic then once that cross-examination is completed hopefully to have them all admitted into evidence. That, as I understood, was Your Honours' rulings. So unless I am told that this is not the way I am to do it, that is the way I propose to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine. The documents are yours still, so we are not in a position to tell you just how to organise them, but the suggestion we made was made in order to try and see if it was possible to somehow regroup the documents according to their substance, to their contents, because as Mr. Zecevic correctly pointed out the other day when we discussed this, the documents, if and when admitted into evidence, will ultimately be used for their contents, and that is why we thought that if it was possible to somehow group the documents together in batches according to their contents and the substance that they raise, then that would be preferable because that would enable us to deal with the contents rather than the source. But if you tell us now that this is not possible because the Assembly, of course, discussed all sorts of things and so did the government, then we will -- we will have to accept that. And I understand what you're saying, that this is the best way in which you can think about how to organise the documents. However, if we do that, we -- we immediately recognise that the Defence is facing a serious problem in that they would have to go through each and every one of the documents in order to have the witness's comments on the substance, the contents of the documents, and for that they would then need a lot more time. And I think if we can't do it any other way, then the Chamber's preference is then to allow the Defence more time. That's the least painful way in which we can get through this. If any of the parties can suggest any better way, then let us hear, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say this, that Mr. Zecevic and I, it's not that we failed to have discussions, it's just at the moment we haven't really had the opportunity to reach an agreement, but our view is that the simplest way of dealing with these types of documents is to simply agree that they go in. There's no challenge, as I understand it, leaving aside intercepts, but to the records of the -- no challenge to the authenticity of the records of the Assembly minutes, the government minutes, and the like, and we could, therefore, simply agree between us and present the Trial Chamber with a package of all of these documents, and then each of us in turn would address, when the time came, Your Honours on what we said were the relevant matters in favour of either side's submissions on these matters, and that is a way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Isn't that exactly what we are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, because we don't mean just these. We mean all of them. There are -- this is only a selection, I'm sorry to have to tell you, of some of the Assembly minutes that are on our list. Others are allocated to be dealt with by Mr. Trbojevic and other witnesses. But we can simply avoid all that, put them all in a package. But as I say, Mr. Zecevic and I haven't worked this out fully yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, it seems to me that what you're suggesting is to have them admitted merely by their authenticity --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- by their reliability. But admission into evidence for the Chamber involves two tests, namely not only reliability but also relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. May I say straight away, I mean, that says it itself. They are relevant. Even -- Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just finish this. I have the feeling you think the Prosecution is just trying to throw in documents, if I can put in the vernacular, for the hell of it. We're not. We're as anxious as the Trial Chamber to limit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. Mrs. Korner, let me be sure that we understand each other correctly. We're not afraid of evidence. That's the way you make it sound. But what we are keen to try and do throughout this trial is to ensure that whenever we admit a piece of evidence that, we have had the chance to understand the evidentiary value it has in relation to your indictment, and rather than just admitting a huge load of documents into evidence and then only after the trial having to start reading these documents during our deliberations, rather than doing that, we really would prefer if in the process of admitting the evidence, that we can be shown by the party who brings the evidence, and this is not only the Prosecution, it also goes for the Defence, what the evidentiary value is of this particular piece of evidence so as to be able to assess right there and then, and particularly when we have witnesses who can testify and who can provide comments to the evidence, to have this possibility as we admit the evidence. So this is why we are trying to find or device a way in which we can have these huge loads of documents admitted into evidence without necessarily having to go into each one of them but still having an understanding of what these documents really tend to show in relation to the crimes and to the charges raised against the two accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, we do understand that. The difficulty is this: Your Honours -- or you as the Pre-Trial Judge, took the view that a short trial was what was required. If you want a short trial, then -- and I don't mean you, I mean you the Trial Chamber, then what has to be dispensed with sometimes is the minute examination, if you like, or even indeed a certain level of examination of each individual piece of evidence, because that takes time. There is no -- there's no other way of dealing with it than other -- as has happened in previous trials where, for example, witnesses -- this particular witness who was called by the Court in Krajisnik testified over a period roughly of four days, although it doesn't appear to have been full days. One of the witnesses coming testified for nine days in chief and cross-examination because he was taken through every document so that the Trial Chamber could see why it was relevant. Now, because of the time constraints, one of the ways I think that Your Honours would have to sacrifice is knowing exactly the relevance of every piece -- every document you admit and leaving it to counsel when they address Your Honours at the relevant time to pull together, and that is our duty, to pull together the parts of the documents that we say are relevant to a particular issue that you're going to have to rule on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In our understanding, that is exactly what we are now suggesting, that you go ahead as we have ruled. Namely, that you introduce these eight different batches of documents, and you show the witness and you show the Chamber a couple of samples from each batch. And then we leave it to the Defence to, during their cross-examination, raise the points that they take issue with. But since, of course, the Defence has to be concerned more about the substance and the contents of the documents, we shall have to allow them extra time for that. And as I said, I think this is the least painful way of getting through it. It will inevitably incur some delay in the sense of some extra time is required for this, but I think that is the price that we will then have to pay at this moment. So this may cause in the end a slight extension of the trial time, but hoping that there are not too many witnesses of this kind, I think we can -- we can live with it, and this is the least troublesome option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a brief comment. I hope this -- this doesn't suggest that -- that the burden is reversed, burden of proof, because it is my understanding that it is for our colleagues from the other side to show that the documents are relevant and in fact show and support their thesis in -- or their theory of the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is no reversal of the burden of proof. The burden of proof clearly lies with the Prosecution, and -- and no question can be raised about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In fact, we discussed this very point as we were coming in, and our understanding is that the Prosecution will highlight the relevant parts of the documents, and it is then for the Defence to select those documents that you take issue with and have them -- and challenge their contents while the witness is here. But as I said, we will give you extra time for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. Good morning to you again. First of all, thank you very much for coming to attend, assist the Tribunal as a witness, and on behalf the Chamber and counsel on both sides, I assure you that we will not detain you for one minute longer than is necessary. Could you give us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 20th of November, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your profession is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a university professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you are familiar with the procedure whereby the side calling you would, first of all, have questions for you, in which case it's the Prosecution, followed by the cross-examination, and then the Chamber may have some questions. What is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Serb in the sense of ethnicity, but I am from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If we may have a moment, please, Ms. Korner. Yes, Ms. Korner. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, first of all, can I deal with your previous testimony at this court. I think in 2006, over a period of some four days altogether, you testified in the trial against Momcilo Krajisnik. I'm sorry, you've got to say yes. And just so that we have the record correct, I think it was the Judges who ordered you to appear, and they were the first persons to ask you questions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That's right. I was a court witness then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you would pull your chair up. Thank you very much, Mr. Djeric. And during the course of your testimony you were shown and asked to comment upon a number of documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, may I ask that his previous testimony and the associated exhibits be admitted. They've already been, I understand, pre-marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Tendered, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P179.1 through P179.24, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djeric, just to give a lit bit more background, I think you started out as an economist working for a company called Energoinvest in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then did you become an assistant professor at the university of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: First an assistant professor and then a professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you enter politics, in fact, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, while I was still a student, I was already involved in some kind of youth policies or politics, young student politics. So my first contact with politics was while I was still a student, but then for a while I was not involved in politics up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in 1991 did you become a member of the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the initial democratic changes in this government in 1991, I was appointed minister without a portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And did you eventually become minister for development?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: This was actually -- I was -- I had this function as a minister without a portfolio. There was no Ministry of Development, but I as a person, my -- the ambit of my work was development, the preparation of development documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you at any stage a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After the government, the Bosnian Serb government, was formed, did you join that government in mid-March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: When the government was being put together, in one of the Assembly sessions of Bosnian Serbs, as you said, I was appointed as prime minister designate. This was in March, and now I realise that it was on the 24th of March, 1992, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And did you take up that position as prime minister from -- at the end of March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was appointed prime minister designate. Your question is rather complex, so I will have to explain it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll tell you what, Mr. Djeric, we have limited time, so don't worry. I appreciate there were a number of steps, but you became the prime minister proper in the end, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, first I was prime minister designate, and then I was the president of government, or the prime minister, but there are many formal and practical aspects that we would have to really explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going to ask you to explain in a moment or two about the various aspects of the government in its largest form, but can I just move to the end now. Did you in fact tender your resignation at the end of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was at the Prijedor session, if I am not mistaken. This session was, as I learnt later, on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. However --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: But this is something that you would have to check, because I'm not really good with dates, and I really could not check that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And -- well, we're going to -- one of the documents I'm going to show you is the session that was at the end of November of 1992. Was it then that your -- you actually resigned, or your resignation was accepted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No. I submitted my resignation at the end of October, on the 29th of September, but please don't take this date literally. This happened at the session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Prijedor. At the end of October I signed it and submitted it. I don't know the reasons why this was not discussed at that session of the Assembly and why my resignation was not accepted then. It was actually postponed for another -- to be discussed at another session in November, as you said, and that's when it was accepted. But I officially and in writing submitted my resignation on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Actually, I don't know whether it was a mistake in the translation but it says 29th of September at page 45, line 7, but it was October. All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Djeric. If you feel you must, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about the dates. I was just telling you. It was at the Prijedor session of the Assembly where I submitted my written resignation, but it was actually accepted at the session in Zvornik, but I'm not sure of the dates. All of this happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Well, that's -- that's the preliminaries. Now, I want you to have a look, please, at a chart that's been prepared of the -- the Republic of Serbia government in Bosnia and just confirm for us, would you. It's 10138.3.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. This was the Government of Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Because you said of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. It's going to come up on the screen in front of you. Right. And I want you to, as we go through it, can you explain perhaps briefly, Mr. Djeric, the set-up, as it were, of the government. We see at the top there was the Republika Srpska Presidency, Dr. Koljevic, Dr. Karadzic, and Dr. Plavsic. How -- what was the function of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it is unclear about the Presidency. Maybe that's how it was described in some laws in peacetime there, but while we were there, this was really a sort of coordinating body of a number of officials of the Serbian people. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: And these are the most prominent officials of the Serbian people, and I would refer to it really as a coordinating body, because in the event of war, and it was stated clearly in the law, it would say that there would be a Presidency in wartime. However, a state of war was never declared, so that the legal status of this body is really unclear and I can't shed any right on that. I'm not a professional lawyer, so I don't really know. I can only confirm that these were the most prominent officials of the Serbian people at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And was Dr. Karadzic the president of the Presidency, as it were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Excuse me? Well, that was his role. He was a party man, and he was at the head of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: But in fact, in keeping with the law that the head of this there should have been Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic, because they were elected by popular vote in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how was Dr. Karadzic elected then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was the president of the party and the president of the council for national security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, we'll come on to that in a moment when we start to look on the -- then we see what is called the expanded Presidency, which includes the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, and then yourself as president of the government. How did the expanded Presidency work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, we came -- I came when invited, so at first this body functioned as a National Security Council. So there was some actually unclear -- unclear distinctions between what the bodies were. Often they didn't meet. You would get called, and then the conversations would take a different course. You would just stay there waiting for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- I don't want to stop you, Dr. Djeric, but all I'm concerned about at the moment is if the Presidency was expanded to include you and Mr. Krajisnik, did that mean that you would attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That meant that I was obliged to attend whenever issues that would be something that was within my competence were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now that's the next question I was going to ask you. What was within your competence as prime minister or president of the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: For the most part we dealt with economic issues, social issues, information, cultural problems, social and so on. Other than these matters -- so all those matters that did not deal and had nothing to do with the war sector. That was not something that was within my competence, the command functions and everything that had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did the government interact with the Assembly? In other words, would the government carry out the wishes of the Assembly, or -- however it voted, or would the government bring forward matters to the Assembly or both?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we prepared materials and documents, laws, regulations, and so on, for the Assembly. In other words, we prepared for the Assembly sessions, and at times we would also handle -- if there were any objections to the documents or proposals, we would have to work on that. So basically it was the legislative aspect that was something that I had to deal with and my ministers.
