utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we move the chart up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see then the first deputy president or deputy prime minister of the government was a gentleman named Momcilo Pejic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was then replaced in around June of 1992 by Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No? When do you say -- all right. Did Mr. Trbojevic become the deputy president?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Trbojevic was the deputy president. So in other words, they were both vice-presidents, but they were -- they had different competencies. Pejic was in charge of the economics and finances, where Trbojevic -- whereas Trbojevic was in charge of the internal policies. So he coordinated the work of the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior and similar ministries. So that was Trbojevic's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then we see that the minister of internal affairs was Mico Stanisic. The minister of the defence was Colonel Subotic, and the minister of foreign affairs was Buha. Now, around these gentlemen, and we'll have a look in a moment at the National Security Council minute, but they are shown as part of the National Security Council. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't really figure this out. There are a lot of different charts here. I mean, the government was separate, and here we have it all in one, so I'm not really clear. But I can tell you that within the framework of the government Buha was minister of foreign affairs, Subotic was the minister of defence, Mico Stanisic -- Stanisic is the minister of internal affairs, and these were the two deputy presidents. As for the Security Council and that aspect, I'm really not in a position to explain that very well, simply because this is not something that was within my competence, so I really don't know. It was a bit farther removed from me. So I don't know what they did at the Security Council, because this is something that Karadzic was really at the head of, so I can't really discuss this. And I don't know what division of functions was within the security council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just move down to the rest of the chart. And we see there listed the other ministers in the government during this period. The only one at the moment I want to mention is Momcilo Mandic as minister of justice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but this is an exhaustive list of ministers, but they actually came at different times. I don't know exactly when Momcilo Mandic was appointed. Maybe that was in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see the appointment of Momcilo Mandic at some other stage. All right, I just want to -- finally on this, before I deal with the various, as it were, committees or governments, to whom should Mico Stanisic as minister of internal affairs, to whom should he have reported?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: He had a twofold role, in fact. For the military issues he was -- he reported to the supreme commander, or in other words, to Karadzic who was at the head of this. As for the other tasks that fell in the scope of the Ministry of the Interior, then this he would have reported to the president of the government for this. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So -- yes. If the police were going to be used for military matters, he would report to Karadzic. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: And everything that had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Because I did not have the authority to order the employment of the police or the milicija, in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for other matters, that is to do with straight, as it were, policing matters, he would report to you, is that right, or should have reported to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, he should have for all those questions that have to do with the legislative aspects, financing, the budget, and so forth. These issues, he was supposed to coordinate the work in these aspects with the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's start, then, looking at some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions at this stage on the functioning of the government and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I believe part of the answer by witness has not been recorded in the transcript. I wouldn't like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, I'm sorry, I was looking at something else. Part of which answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Part of the answer on -- the last answer, page 51, 12 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Djeric, we'll go back over this for a moment. I asked you whether for straight policing matters he reported to you, or should have reported to you, and the answer as recorded was: "Well, he should have for all those questions that have to do with the legislative aspects, financing, the budget, and so forth. These issues he was supposed to coordinate the work in these aspects with the president of the government." Did you add anything else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, I said first of all he would coordinate them with the deputy president of government for internal affairs, and that was Trbojevic because he was in charge of this ministry, and then the next step would be with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right. Can we look, then, please, at the Assembly meeting which dealt with your appointments and that of Mr. Stanisic. It's 65 ter 921, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could have the first page up in each case just so that we can -- in the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that this was the Bosnian Serb Assembly meeting on the -- I'm -- just a -- oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You need to -- sorry, the B/C/S needs to go -- the page needs to go further up, please. I want to go down the page on the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Shows it was a meeting that was held on the 24th of March in Pale. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your microphone's not on, Mr. Djeric. Yes, it's on now. I'm afraid you'll have to repeat your answer. You've had the opportunity of looking through this, haven't you, Mr. Djeric? Have you -- Mr. Djeric, can you see on the screen you've got some documents -- a document, I hope. Can you just confirm you've had the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the third page in B/C/S and in English -- actually, second page first of all. I'm so sorry. The second page. Third page in B/C/S, second page in English. Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Milan Milanovic says that the Council of Ministers of the Assembly -- or, rather, the decision to relieve from duty -- "The Council of Ministers of the Assembly of the Serbian people which was established on the 21st of December, 1991, is hereby relieved from duty."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, mine won't turn off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I just noted that -- that the witness has not been asked by Ms. Korner whether he would give the same answers if he was asked. So now I would -- I need to raise that as an objection now, because the situation is developing in that -- in that aspect. I mean, because the -- because the documents have been tendered and his statement before, and he wasn't asked if he would give the same answers to the questions as before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic is quite right. I did -- I did omit to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Djeric, I'm sorry to -- Mr. Djeric, I'm sorry to stop you dealing with this document for the moment. Was your testimony that you gave in the Krajisnik case read back to you a few days ago now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I actually leafed through it. Yes, I did have occasion to review it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In the event that you were to be asked those questions again, was what was in those -- what was in the record of that an accurate record of what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Such was your previous testimony as you reviewed, were you able to, I suppose, remember that that was an accurate record of what you told the Trial Chamber and the various people who asked you questions at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I think so. I told the truth then, and I am still telling the truth. Maybe there's something that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. As you heard, Mr. Zecevic wanted that question asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I wanted to stand up. I think the proper -- the proper question to the witness is whether he will give the very same answers to the questions posed to him at that time today. That is the question that the witness has to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we have to discuss it, which I think we may have, then I think the witness needs to leave court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, this is a procedure concerning 92 ter and the jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, it would seem to us that the suggestions made by Mr. Zecevic would be just straightforward according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, in that event, I think I do need to discuss. There's a good reason why I haven't asked the question in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, we would kindly ask you, Dr. Djeric, to leave us for a short period of time. The usher will take you out, and we'll bring you back shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I think we should go into private session. [Private session] Confidentiality lifted by oral order of the Chamber

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know what the rule says. The difficulty with this witness is the following, and Your Honours may have seen it when you read through it: He gives completely contradictory answers from questions in some respects that he's asked on the same topic, firstly, when the Judges asked him questions, and secondly, when Mr. Tieger for the Prosecution was cross-examining him, and it is directly the contrary. For example, at one stage he's shown the signature on the document, says it's a forgery, and then another stage when he's shown the document again he says, no, it isn't a forgery, I agree it's my signature. So to ask him the question as it's phrased under the rules, would you give the same answers is to ask him, would you give directly contradictory answers in some cases, and that seems to me it doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if that is the case which Ms. Korner is explaining right now, then it's not admissible. They -- the Prosecution choose to lead this witness as a 92 ter witness with the 92 ter package. The rules are very explicit. The witness has to answer whether today he will give the same answers to the same questions. That has to be done. Otherwise, all this package which was admitted as an exhibit will not -- is not admissible according to the rule. They could have called him as a viva voce witness. That was the option. Or don't call him at all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course I can ask him the question in those terms. That's what the rules mean, but it -- it's going to look pretty silly is all I can say. I can certainly ask him that question. It seems to me that the real gravamen of all of this was that the answers he gave then are those as are recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We did not become aware of some of the inconsistencies until we started reading a couple of days ago, but that was when you had introduced him as a 92 ter witness, and I must say that now that the full story is being disclosed, it is -- I think maybe he should have been called as a viva voce witness, because the -- the conditions under which you can bring 92 ter witnesses are those that follow from the rule. But let us just consult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber, having heard the explanation of counsel for the Prosecution and being alive to the concerns raised by Mr. Zecevic, considers that where we're at now with this witness, we just -- we will continue, and the -- it will be for the -- when the turn of the Defence comes, no doubt that they would do what they think best to do in terms of what of the material -- the whole body of material they have available before them, both the exhibit of the -- being the witness's prior testimony, and what he says here today. We see no other practical way out of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And could I just add, Mrs. Korner, that since he was introduced as a 92 ter witness and we have admitted the testimony, then, you know, that's the track that you have set us on, and this means that you have to put the questions to him that are required under 92 ter. There's no way around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a matter of practical reality, of course, but can I say that I completely forgot to ask the question, but I was going to ask it in the way I suggested, but I will ask him the question as required by the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But can I just -- either you bring him as a viva voce or you bring him as a 92 ter, but there's no way in between that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I -- I mean, the Rule 92 ter(A)(3)is very clear, I think, and what we're -- in this situation, what has been done by the Prosecution is noncompliance with the Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we have the witness back in, please. And we're back if public session, open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I just want to ask you one further question in respect of your previous testimony. I've already asked you whether it accurately reflects what you said. Secondly, if you were asked the same questions again today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I am speaking the truth, and in that sense I would give the same answer. I don't know if I would use exactly the same words, but I would give the same answer. I have come here to speak the truth, but there is a problem here if I can indicate it, about the end of duty of the ministerial council, because these people who were dismissed from duty were no longer working in that particular way, but I was told that if I wish to pick any of them for ministerial posts, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about that. I just want to ask you -- the reason I've shown you that is what was the Council of Ministers of the Assembly of the Serbian People, which was, as it were, abolished in this Assembly session? What was its role?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: This was an executive organ of the Assembly or of the parliament of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did it operate as its -- if I can put it that way, its unofficial government before the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No. The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared at the Assembly in January 1992. It was proclaimed then. The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was the name. And it exists in the documents. It already adopted its constitution as of January, and it had its executive body just like states today have a council of ministers. That would be the equivalent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what was the reason for its abolition in March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, this would require a longer answer, but I will try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, since the witness is about to go into what may not be a brief explanation, we notice it's 12.05 so this may be a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought it was 12.20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give a short answer as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A short answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can provide a short answer. Simply, there were some political changes that occurred. You know that at the time negotiations were under way and that the international community had offered the Cutileiro Plan based on the offer by the diplomat Cutileiro. So then the leadership of the Serbian people or the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided in order to complete the process of democratisation and to monitor the plan, they decided to reinforce their organs and to transform the Council of Ministers into a government. So for those political goals, the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina required a government and not a council of ministers. So this was done for the reason of democratisation, for reasons of decentralisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in order to coordinate with the international community regarding the implementation of the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I apologise. So the government was formed exclusively with peacetime intentions. This is something that needs to be kept in mind, for peacetime purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, while the witness is on his way back in, could you at a convenient point, let's say about two minutes before the time of adjournment, break your examination there? We'll alert you as to the dies non juridicus for the record, whatever the plural is in Latin for the rest of the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, they abolished Latin in English some time ago, so I've forgotten all the Latin I've learned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, still on the -- this Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the second page in B/C/S and the third page in English. Actually, no, back to the last page in B/C/S. I don't know why that -- I see, because the numbering at the top is not the same. Can we go back, I'm sorry, to the last -- that's it, but we need page 2 in English. Okay. Well, that's not -- page 3 then, please. Different page numbers. Page 3. Sorry. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that the Council of Ministers included yourself at number 7. Number 3 just to note, Dr. Zepinic, and at number 19 Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go, please, in the B/C/S to page 4 and in the English to page 5. To the bottom of page 4 in B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You there -- you spoke, Mr. Djeric, and you started by saying that you had completed your consultations, consulting with the presidents of the Serb autonomous districts. What were you consulting with the presidents of the Serb autonomous districts about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: What is being discussed here is the forming of the government, candidates and so on. So I spoke. I assume, I don't see it here, but I spoke in the sense that I wanted to point to a certain procedure, that it was necessary to carry out certain consultations. And if I don't -- if I remember correctly, at that time I put forward the names of two candidates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you did, and we'll go to the next page, but I just want for a moment to stick with the -- in the next page in B/C/S, please, which is page 4. So you were consulting with the presidents of the SAOs about candidates for government ministers. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: These were people who were deputies in any event at the Assembly of the Serbian People there. I didn't go and travel around the areas to do the consultations. This was all done in the break between the -- of the Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you specifically mentioned them. Does that mean that they had some kind of say in who became a government minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: You're thinking of the deputies, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The presidents of the SAOs who, as you say, were also deputies to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, did they have some kind of influence in respect of whom should be appointed a government minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I am not talking about the presidents of the SAOs. I'm talking about the deputies in the Assembly of the Serbian People from different areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it -- it says in the English, and tell me if this is correct: "I have completed my consultation in the meantime, consulting also with the presidents of the Serbian Autonomous Districts ..." And then you go on to propose the two candidates. Now, do you agree you said, according to this record you had been consulting with the presidents of the SAOs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't recall that, but on the basis of this it's possible that we are talking about these two representatives here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go -- I'm sorry, because in the B/C/S, unfortunately it's still on the previous page. We need to go back to page 3. Right. Does the second paragraph say that you've been consulting with the presidents of the SAOs, in your language, in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I also -- after this consultation I noted that they were the presidents of the SAOs. I guess this is where the two candidates came from, from Herzegovina and from the Sarajevo-Romanija region. We're talking about Buha and Mico Stanisic. Of course, at the time the consultations were -- well, first of all, they had to do with the party, with its work and so on and so forth, because the party was the one that was offering the candidates. I apologise. I wasn't able to pick any candidates other than the ones that were put forward by the party. I could perhaps talk about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't -- pause.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: -- it more to get a little bit better acquainted with the candidate --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. First of all, you said you had to put forward the candidates that those were the party -- which party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the only and the ruling party, the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And my question was: Did the presidents of the SAOs of which there were five, have a say in who would get nominated for a minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I assume so, yes, but it was proceeding through the party mechanism. As part of the party certain people were filtered, and specifically I was given these two names: Buha and Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: So I was provided the names, and it's possible that I and the deputies from Herzegovina and from the Sarajevo-Romanija region talked and kind of asked them about these candidates, because I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, I didn't know much, because it was just a brief period of time while these political events were going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you say -- as you say, you corrected yourself. You did know them, didn't you, because they both served with you, for example, on the National Security Council and the Council of Ministers.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say knew here, it's not that I -- well, I don't know somebody much, if I didn't know somebody for a longer period of time, you know. It's superficial acquaintance. And even as part of these consultations it was sort of kind of in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have an intervention in the transcript. I believe the -- 64 -- page 64, 2 to 5, is the answer of Mr. Djeric is recorded and not the question. This can be corrected, please. It is his answer, it is not the question by Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you would have proposed other people for these posts than Stanisic and Buha if you'd been given a free-hand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: For sure. Potentially there could have been other people, but here you were being given people. It was exclusively the offer of the party. So you could, thus, put that forward or not put it forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: The candidates' names were put forward by the party. That's how it was. There was no other mechanism. I didn't have full freedom in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And who from the party told you that you had to propose these two men for these two posts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I think that it was speaking with Karadzic. I was speaking with Karadzic. I don't know if anyone else was there, but as the president of the party, he asked that it be these people, the Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic, and Buha for reasons of a political nature. They needed somebody who was going to affirm Republika Srpska in the international framework as a region, and that is why the ministry for foreign affairs was formed. There was another key ministry, the Ministry of Defence, but they didn't find adequate candidates, so only these two were confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Was the -- how important a ministry was the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well -- well, it should be important, you know, like in any other country, the Ministry of the Interior or internal affairs, but you have to bear in mind that this government and this ministry were just in the process of being established, and there were certain objectives they had. One of those was to promote and affirm the role of Republika Srpska. And just allow me to say one other thing. We have to bear in mind that the government had peacetime objectives, and that is very important. And the minister who was appointed here, that was -- those were his only objectives. And I would like to note it now, because maybe I won't give -- be given an opportunity to do it later, but this government which was being -- in the process of being formed in April and May, they would have remained unless two events happened. This was one -- was the Cutileiro commission and the other there was an attack on a Yugoslav People's Army column in Sarajevo. So these two events actually completely changed the whole situation, and had they not happened, I am -- I can claim with full certainty here that this government would -- that this government would have kept within those frames. What else would have happened, I don't know, because it wasn't -- it was out of our hands, but this minister was not appointed to wage war but, rather, to carry out his duties within the government in Republika Srpska. And you have to bear in mind that we always called it and it was always stressed that this was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So no one was talking about any Serbian state. It was just a question of democratisation within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think you've made your point, Mr. Djeric, on this. Can we move through the rest of this Assembly, please. Mico Stanisic, as we've seen, was proposed by you as was Mr. Buha, and was then the Assembly elected them, and Mico Stanisic made a speech. I want to look, however, at -- at something that was said by another member of the Assembly, Mr. Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look at page 12 in the English, please, and in the B/C/S it is page 9. Page -- yes. Sorry, we need to go -- page 12 in the English needs to come up. I'm sorry. Further down the page, please. Thank you. And I hope we've got it up in the B/C/S now. I'm sorry. Wait a minute. No, page 9 on the -- no, it's one page further. Page 10, sorry -- it's one page further than -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vjestica, is it right that he was president of what was called the Serbian municipality of -- or the Assembly man from Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: He attended the Assembly session, but as for the formal aspects, I'm really not privy to that. I assume that that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he came from Bosanska Krupa. That's all I want you to establish. Do you accept that? Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was from Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: That I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said here that: "... the Assembly should adopt a conclusion instructing the president of the government of the Serbian Republic of Serbia and Bosnia -- Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the ministers to be -- prepare by Friday an operational plan for assuming power, that is, for establishing power in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... particularly in the field of internal affairs," et cetera. Now, first of all, you were the president of the government, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was designate, prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. And he was saying that there should be a plan, an operational plan, for assuming power. Now, what was he referring to when he said "an operational plan for assuming power," particularly in the light of what you've just said, this was meant to be a peaceful Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was referring to, but I can tell you that in January, I think in January of 1992, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed, and I think that it was either then or -- well, possibly then the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted, and the political objectives were to strengthen the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but the territory that was being claimed was not only that of Serbs, was it, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, clearly no one ever had any issue with that. What we're talking about here is the Serbian Republic of -- Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you have a unitary state which cannot move forward until some political issues are resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Djeric, is your answer to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: As to what this gentleman was referring to specifically, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but he was referring to you specifically. So did you ask him at any stage what he wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, no. He clearly states here that this is what needs to be done. This is his proposal at the Assembly session. This is his contribution to the discussion. He is saying here what the president of the government and the ministers are to do, and this is what he's proposing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Well, let's have a look at what your response to this was, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move in the English to page 13, and in the B/C/S to page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you said Dr. -- Mr. Djeric, was: "The government will have a duty to draw up an operational plan and submit it for adoption. We shall do our best to speed things up, to gain time wherever possible. There is no reason to think we are running late in assuming power, because a lot has been accomplished by now. Please do not take things into your own hands. You will receive your instructions and you will proceed as instructed." Now, what did you mean, first of all, by the fact that you were going to speed things up to gain time wherever possible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind was the peace plan of the international community, the Cutileiro Plan. This was the proposal that was offered to us. The constitution and the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina were offered, certain functions were offered so that in fact this plan was in a certain sense the implementation of the Cutileiro Plan which would be favourable to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: So the basis for this was this international document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. What about the words "Please do not take things into your own hands. You will receive your instructions"? What was concerning you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, what was concerning me was that there was a certain disorderly conduct of some people who were trying to do things on their own to actually take political action without coordination, and this was something that gave rise to my concern, and that is why I said that people shouldn't do that, because they were to know how everything was envisaged with this -- within this Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What disorderly conduct are you describing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, most of these people were ordinary people who saw politics as certain practices. How should I put this? There was even a certain degree -- there was a certain degree of tension, because -- I have to remind you of what time we're talking about here. This was from the 1st of March, 1992, and onwards when the Serbian people was voted over by the other two ethnic groups, and this was against the constitutional provisions. In other words, the Serbian people, the rights of the Serbian people, were put in jeopardy, and there was a certain revolt among -- there was a certain dynamics in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is why I was saying here that no one should take things into their own hands or make -- take measures on their own, because they should not actually give priority to the local government but, rather, they should keep within the framework of the higher authorities. So there was the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities, and then there were also the authorities on the ground. So what is important here is the referendum of March 1st.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All that I'm asking you is about the disorderly practices. Are you talking about people seizing power by force?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, to be honest there was some functioning authorities, some functioning local government there. As of March, there was still the army. Troops were still there. So it's not as if there was no government at all. But there was a certain fear. People felt afraid, existentially afraid, and this could have led to some of the parts of Bosnia to sort of assume power or grant power and give their own priority to that of the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- Bosnia and Herzegovina. These processes arose --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Was it clear to you and only -- I'm only asking about you, Mr. Djeric, that if the Cutileiro Plan failed, there was likely to be violence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I was just thinking that if this plan failed, then there would come other plans. Well, you know, politics is a process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because did you know that in the territory of the planned Serbian state in Bosnia there were people living who were not Serbs and might not like the idea of being ruled by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, that is true. There are always people like that. But there's also the fact that the unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina was untenable because it did not provide sufficiently for the Serbian people for their advancement. So this was a question that was to be resolved through political process where these different approaches were to be brought together. So it was natural to express these various interests and also to try and coordinate them through various procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well. All right. Let's leave that document, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I take it that none of the documents are admitted until all of this is finished. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at another document, please, where you did give some instructions, and we'll look at the one that was attached to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have -- I think it's already been marked. P -- well, the 65 ter number was 10036, and the exhibit is now P170.20, I hope. Can we look at -- can we look at the last page, please, in the B/C/S and in the English first of all. All right. Can we go down to the bottom. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that your signature, Mr. Djeric? You saw this document in the Krajisnik case, I think.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: It looks like my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go to the first page then. In English and in B/C/S. Can we see the title. It's called excepts from the instructions on the functioning of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in municipalities. First of all, was there a longer document from which this was taken?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I think it was standard practice to send them out like this. I can't remember. I can't really claim with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you personally draft these instructions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I think it was someone who -- can you tell me when exactly this was? Let me see. The 21st of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I think this was from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 26th of April these ones are dated.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, whether this is from the Ministry of Defence or some other, I really can't recall exactly who was in charge of working on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who told you that these were to go to the municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my assessment that this should be sent to all the participants and all those individuals who were crucial for further developments. I felt responsible, I felt personally responsible to send this because I wanted them to have certain things in mind, to bear in mind that are certain rights, certain laws, certain provisions, conventions, documents that were binding. And that was my only purpose as one of the actors on this political scene. And these Crisis Staffs in municipalities which were unable to convene a meeting, that was also a fact of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, which Crisis Staffs were unable to convene a meeting? Do you mean the Municipal Assembly or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, where the municipal Assembly was in operation, that was the organ. However, where they could not operate, where Municipal Assemblies could not operate, in those cases the Crisis Staffs were the body that was to be informed of what to take care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now the only part of this I want you to have another look at is paragraph 4. So we need to move -- it's all right on B/C/S, but in the English. You -- or, rather, the Ministry of Defence who drafted it but you signed off on it: "The command of the TO and police forces is completely under the competence of professional staff, and therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO and the use of the police forces must be prevented." What was the purpose in putting this paragraph in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was such there were weapons. There was also the Territorial Defence in some areas. Bosnia and Herzegovina was set up in such a way that there was the Yugoslav Army on its territory, but there was also the Territorial Defence that was -- that operated within the framework of the army. So there was a problem here. There was the issue of these various actors interfering and taking over the functions of commanding these territorial forces, police reserves -- reservists, and police and so on. So they were to be clearly told that they were the one who were -- who had the authority to do that, because there was no better way for me to proceed about this but to write this down and send it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, now that's all I want to ask you about that document. Can we move now, please, to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 74, line 18. I think -- I think the witness said in negation to this, not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He said they were to be told that they had no authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not that they had the authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, just to clarify this, you were saying to the Crisis Staffs that they did not have the authority to take over commanding police and territorial forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Nor any party militias or anything of that sort. You understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look then, please, at the next document, 105. Now, on the 30th of April, so some four days after the last document is -- was dated, you sent an order to the Crisis Staffs saying that those instructions weren't valid. This is because "an unfinished text of instructions had been delivered to you by a mistake." Was that what happened, that there should have been a different set of instructions sent to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. And secondly, it wasn't something -- I didn't have the habit of annulling something or destroying something. I don't recall this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's your signature and stamp, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, the signature, it does resemble my own, but the content of this, I don't recall this. It wasn't -- I wasn't in the habit -- I don't know what might have happened here, but I knew what the reasons were for seconding those instructions. But as for this one here, I am not clear on what this document is about, what it was doing here and -- so I didn't have the habit of annulling something. I could add something, but annulling something, that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You may not have been in the habit of it. All I'm asking you at the moment is whether that is your signature and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, the stamp and the signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask about that document. Now, I jumped forward because I wanted to link up your instructions about what was said in the Assembly in March, but I want you to go to another document, the 31st of March of 1992, 65 ter number 61. Unless there's something else you want to say about this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, about the signature, the first part resembles mine, but the rest -- I mean, I think we should really have a handwriting expert here to compare this. I can't really claim this. All I'm claiming is that this was not -- I wasn't in the habit of doing things like this, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, are you suggesting that this document was not sent out by you? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: This one. Well, this wasn't something that I normally did within the framework of my job, but I can't really recall what this would have been caused by, what would have -- what could have been the reason for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Djeric, I don't propose to take this any further on this document, so can we look at another document, please, which is -- I'm sorry, the number was changed. It's not -- it's not -- it was -- it's 10135. Right. This is an extract from "Glas" newspaper, 31st of March, 1992. Were you familiar with "Glas"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's headed "Zepinic called off from BH MUP." And it says: "Today we learned from confidential sources that the Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS called off - I think it means fired - Dr. Vitomir Zepinic from the position of deputy minister of the interior. We acquire this information after -- this English translation beggars belief -- the new mandate of the government of the Serbian Republic. Professor Djeric talked to Dr. Zepinic. All I want to know is, was this newspaper report accurate? Had in fact Dr. Zepinic been, as it were, removed after he'd spoken to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No, because I never spoke with him. He was being recalled by the party for some reason. I don't know which reasons. I don't know if it was a question of confidence or -- because he was an old cadre who was no longer suitable for new changes, democratic changes, and so on and so forth. I don't know, but I didn't speak with him at all, so all this is just journalist's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then I won't take that any further. Thank you. Then I omitted -- I just want you to confirm, could you look, please, very quickly at 65 ter 28. I jumped ahead a bit. That was in the gazette, and it's 21st of December decision showing you as number 6 on the Ministerial Council, Mico Stanisic at number 18, and Dr. Zepinic as number 2. Now, next can we look, please, at the constitution as it was published that you already mentioned, which is 65 ter -- 65 ter 49. If we look at the first page in the B/C/S and the English to begin with. Published in the gazette on the 16th of March of 1992. And could we go, please, to Article 12 onwards, which is the second page in the B/C/S and the third page in the English. Article 12: "No one can be deprived of or limited in freedom except in cases and compliance with the procedures provided for by law." Article 14: "No one may be subjected to torture, cruel inhuman or humiliating treatment ..." Article 15: "Unlawful deprivation of freedom is punishable. "No one may be deprived of freedom without a court decision ..." And "A person suspected of having a criminal offence ..." et cetera. Now, Mr. Djeric, as events went on in 1992 were those articles of the constitution adhered to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No. I think we're all aware that simply many things were going on there. That is, you know, the way that the constitution requires.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And just on one other article, 80 -- sorry, well, two other articles. Article 81, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: But with the following remark: I was finding that out on the basis of certain information that was addressed to the government, and we reacted pursuant to those -- the information. I wasn't able to find out what the situation was in reference to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look at -- I'm sorry, I should have given you the page number. Article 81 is on the B/C/S at page -- I don't know. 0040-8011 at the top, and in the English at page 13. Yes, you've got it. That says that: "In the event of a state of war or immediate threat of war, the president of the republic shall at his own initiative or on a proposal from the government pass enactments on questions falling within the jurisdiction of the Assembly which enactments he shall give to the National Assembly for confirmation as soon as it's able to convene." Was -- what was your understanding of what that meant, of what powers were given to the president by the constitution in the event of an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: He was at the head of the council for national security, and the task of that council was to take care of the security of the people and so on and so forth, and in that sense, you know, to take certain actions and to propose certain documents, regulations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did that give him power -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: And thus when the Assembly was unable to convene, he was performing this function while it, you know, would be able to convene. He was the -- he was the executive organ, and at the same time carrying out the function of the Assembly. And many regulations were sent to him for signature. What was not possible -- what the Assembly could not verify, he would sign and proclaim those regulations to be in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at, understand from you, is your understanding of this, that in a time of immediate threat of war the president had the power to make laws without consulting the Assembly or to make decisions without consulting the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Not that -- it was not a question of consulting, but just when the Assembly was unable to convene, then he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: The Assembly was unable to convene because for different reasons you didn't have the communications required throughout the whole territory. You were not absolutely sure that you would be able to reach the venue and so on and so forth. It was this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, please, on the constitution, Article 100, which is page 17 of the English, and the page in the B/C/S is -- it's got -- it's 0040-8012. It says: "Regions shall be organised in the republic as political and territorial units and cities and municipalities as local units of self-management." And then under Article 104, the regional Assembly. At this stage and we're talking about March of 1992, was regionalisation a part of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: This was an issue -- well, if you speak about regions here, then thus it is a question of the constitutional capacity, local administration and so on and so forth. Thus this simply existed as a -- as a possibility in the constitution. That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: It's a -- it's an Assembly matter adopted the way it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is at this stage in March 1992, was regionalisation envisioned as part of the political structure, if you like, of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: It existed as an idea, as an idea. Of course, based on the principles of some kind of regional and world peace. What we were trying constantly to do here is to implement a certain regionalisation that suited the Serbian people but with agreements, you know, through certain political procedures and compromises. And I said earlier that we hoped that this all would pass nicely, but some events happened which could not be controlled and which threw the government and all of us right into a different track. We did have the intention to work on a serious effort at regionalisation in accordance with the European experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just waiting until you'd finished. I wondered whether you had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was wondering in Article 80 it is said -- it is said that the president of the republic, and so you know, you were just discussing this with the witness. Who was the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very good -- actually I'm just taking -- I was just assuming that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, could you tell the Court who was the president of the republic. I don't know that we ever mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that we're talking about here. First the constitution was adopted, and then work -- further work proceeds pursuant to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, stop, stop, stop, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: We -- we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just wait. All you're being asked is who was the president of the republic? Give us the name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I am telling you the president of the republic at this point in time did not even exist. What did exist were two members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Republika Srpska, and we continued to consider them as -- as the presidents. You understand. So one thing is the document, but the sources were never extrapolated according to the constitution for the president of the republic. There was just the constitutional capacity, thus the potential. Biljana Plavsic and Professor Koljevic were members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that means a certain, let me put it that way --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, but the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: -- part of the collective Presidency that belongs to the Serbian Republic so you're asking me something on the topic of the constitution and I'm not really well-versed in the constitution topics. I could present my opinion here but these are legal and constitutional procedures. All I am doing is recalling that at that time we did not have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to know, Mr. Djeric, nothing more. But there was Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic as well in the Presidency, but he was only, if I may say, president of the party. So that means more or less that this was functioning like a one-party state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a party state that was functioning in which the president of the party was carrying out all the functions practically. We're going to speak about that. You will see. Practically he was the government too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The constitution that we've looked at, however, it's clear, envisaged one person as president of the republic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That's all that I needed to ask you about the constitution. Can we move on now, please, to one of the other -- oh, well perhaps we'll just -- we'll just note in passing, because it refers to the state, immediate threat of war, and can we look, please, briefly at 65 ter number 84, please. This is a -- the Official Gazette actually for the 12th to the 17th of May, but it published at 1 -- at item 142 the decision to declare an immediate threat of war, and that was on the 15th of April. And as we can see, in fact going back to Judge Delvoie's question, it's actually signed "Presidency," Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I was telling you earlier. The constitution provides for certain solutions. Those solutions need to be reached. And this is already a time, you know, when there were no elections for the president, but we had these two persons there who were carrying out the role of members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Did you attend the 12th of May Assembly which was held in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. We've already looked at it with another witness, so I just want to ask you about a document that came out of it. 65 ter 118, please. This appears to be something -- a draft for the gazette, the Official Gazette, setting out the six strategic goals that were enunciated at the 12th of May Assembly. Do you remember hearing about the six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I did hear of that, but I wasn't really involved in that. At that Assembly there was talk or discussion about that. I think for the first time was -- that was, I think, the first time that I heard about that. These are more party, SDS party goals and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All I want to ask you about this is apparently it was drafted -- it wasn't actually sent to -- it wasn't published in the gazette for some considerable time. Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because it's not in my jurisdiction. I wasn't really dealing with that, and I don't know, and I wouldn't have then, nor would I today have agreed with much that is said here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't agree with those goals.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]. Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this figured, you know, but what I'm saying, you know, simply there is much here that is -- you know, has nothing to do with anything. It's not in the spirit of the times and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think you're going to have to explain that a little bit more, Mr. Djeric. What -- just a moment. Wait for the question. Did you or did you not agree with those goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I did not express my opinion on these matters. This was not submitted to the government. This was not in my purview. I'm speaking about it generally. And as for my agreement and disagreement then had I been in the position, and now I would not have agreed with that. Well, look at this division of the town of Sarajevo. I mean, after Berlin there can be no division of cities. I knew that then and I knew this now. This is more of a rural option by some rural politicians who were imagining Sarajevo as the urban part and some sort of rural environs of that town and the division of cities. Anybody who is barely literate would know that this is something that is unfitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what did you understand was supposed to happen with Sarajevo? What did the division of Sarajevo mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you understand when you heard this was meant to happen in Sarajevo which you think was impossible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Any politician worth his salt, any serious political factor would not think in a way like this, you understand. You need to take care that -- at that time we have the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thus, what division of Sarajevo? I mean, it's another matter the organisation of the state and so on, but division of Sarajevo simply is something that does not have much sense, much logic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Division of Sarajevo into what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I am -- it says here. I'm giving you my opinion. I didn't sign this. I didn't agree with this. I didn't work on the implementation of this and so on and so forth. You understand. So I don't know. You would need to ask those who were putting this forward. I am unable to interpret the policy of the SDS or the SDS president, this one or that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Djeric. You've just said the division of the city of Sarajevo was impossible. What division do you mean was impossible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Any kind of division. A town is a town. A city is a city. It's an entity. I'm thinking of any kind of division. How are you going to divide a town? Another thing is, you know, policies regarding these or those interests, but something that had to do with division of a town. It's something that really wouldn't be able to go through, and I assure you that the people in Sarajevo of Serb ethnicity or thereabouts, that was something that was out of the question. People were surprised. They were flabbergasted with some of these solutions that were accepted in relation to Sarajevo and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Well, if we look at the actual number 5, it says: "Division of the city of Sarajevo into -- on Serbian and Muslim part and creation." Are you saying that it was impossible the way that Sarajevo was inhabited to separate them into Serbian and Muslim parts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: It wasn't possible. It simply wasn't possible, and it could not have figured, you know, as a goal. This is what I'm talking about. I don't know who thought of what and whose idea it was to initiate these goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: These were not goals of a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Of a general -- but there were -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think in view of the time you asked for that's probably an appropriate moment before I move to another document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- your testimony has -- has a way to go yet, so you are excused but not released. Because you are sworn as a witness, you cannot discuss your testimony with the lawyers from either side, and in your conversations with anyone outside the Chamber, you can talk about anything else but not your testimony here. Do you understand what I've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're excused to return to this Chamber at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. For the benefit of counsel and to give advance notice to the parties, the dates that have been decided on, and this is picking up where we left off yesterday, would be Monday the 9th of November, Monday the 30th of November, and I would remind the parties that that follows upon the Friday the 27th, which is a UN holiday, and then Friday the 18th of December. So the lawyers can, in terms of their witnesses, arrange their -- make the arrangements accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour, for that indication. We'll -- we'll -- that's -- so I'm assuming that means that all the outstanding motions will be completed by Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hopefully before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
